platforms.title: Low-Temperature Burn Signs: The Lace-Pattern Rash Explained
platforms.meta_description: A reddish, lace-like rash from a heating pad isn't just irritation — it's a low-temperature burn called erythema ab igne. Here's how to spot it early.
platforms.body_html:
A heating pad set on low, used night after night, doesn't feel dangerous. But skin exposed to 43-47°C (109-117°F) for hours at a time can develop a distinctive reddish, net-like rash that doctors call erythema ab igne — literally "redness from fire." It's a genuine low-temperature burn, not a mild irritation, and it's easy to miss because there's rarely a moment of sharp pain to flag it. Case reports collected in the U.S. National Library of Medicine describe it appearing after weeks or months of the same nightly habit, long after anyone would think to connect a warm blanket to skin damage.

Why the Rash Looks Like a Net, Not a Blotch

According to those case reports, erythema ab igne starts as blotchy redness and evolves into a reticulated (lace- or net-patterned) mark that follows the blood vessels closest to the heat source. The pattern itself is a clue — a fishnet-shaped mark on a thigh, lower back, or abdomen is a strong sign of repeated heating-pad contact, even if the person doesn't remember falling asleep with it on. Space heaters, heated car seats, and laptops resting on the lap for long stretches can leave the same kind of mark, so the location often points to the actual source.

Why Older Adults and People With Diabetes Are Most at Risk

A case report published in American Family Physician described erythema ab igne developing in a patient with diabetic neuropathy — nerve damage that dulls the ability to feel heat building up. Reduced sensation means the usual warning signal (skin starting to feel uncomfortably hot) simply doesn't arrive in time, so the pad stays in place for hours instead of the 20 minutes generally recommended for heat therapy. Thinner, more fragile skin in older adults also means the same amount of heat does more damage than it would in younger skin.

Cut the Exposure Time, Not Just the Temperature

Turning the dial down helps, but temperature alone isn't the full story — duration matters just as much. Set a timer instead of relying on how the skin feels, and never fall asleep with a heating pad still running, even on the lowest setting. If a heating pad doesn't have an auto shut-off, unplug it manually before settling in for the night, and keep a layer of fabric between the pad and bare skin rather than placing it directly against the body.

Check the Skin, Not Just the Setting

Look at the area under the heating pad in daylight once a week, especially for anyone with diabetes, poor circulation, or nerve damage. Mild redness usually fades within days once the heat source is removed. If the mottled pattern persists for weeks, turns dark or scaly, or a sore spot won't heal, that's a reason to see a dermatologist — case reviews note that in rare, long-standing cases, chronically damaged skin can undergo changes that need medical evaluation rather than being left to resolve on its own.

Tonight, before the heating pad goes on: set a 20-minute timer. That single habit removes the exposure time that turns ordinary warmth into a lace-pattern burn.
